pedagogy.summary: Children learn to pick the right standard unit and instrument for what they are measuring — length (m/cm), mass (kg/g), temperature (°C), capacity (l/ml) — and to measure to the nearest sensible unit. The skill has two joined parts: first name the attribute (how long? how heavy? how much fills it?) so the unit family matches, then choose the grain that yields a readable, precise number (a pencil in cm, not m; a drink in ml, not litres).
bestPractices: Name the attribute before choosing a unit — length, mass, temperature or capacity — so the unit family and the instrument match what is being measured.
Teach grain choice explicitly: which unit gives a sensible, readable number for THIS object (cm for a pencil, m for a room), using benchmark sizes to judge.
Establish why standard units at all — contrast two children's hand-spans giving different counts — so children see standard units let everyone compare.
Give a mixed 'measuring station' across all four attributes so choosing (not just reading) is the practised act.
Introduce standard units once the need is understood; the progression warns that heavy early use of many varied non-standard units can actually interfere with grasping why standard units are needed.
keyRepresentations: A measuring station: ruler/tape, kitchen scale, measuring jug, thermometer, with unit dials m/cm, kg/g, l/ml, °C
Benchmark objects for each unit (a metre stick, a 1 kg bag, a 1 litre bottle)
A sorting chart matching everyday objects to their sensible unit
The 'same object, different hand-spans' contrast motivating standard units
commonMisconceptions: Uses a unit or tool from the wrong attribute — e.g. reaches for a ruler to find 'how much water', or gives grams for a length.
Picks the wrong grain — measures a pencil in metres ('0 m') or a room laboriously in centimetres — not choosing to the nearest appropriate unit.
Happily reports a non-standard count ('6 cubes') when a standard measurement is asked for, not seeing why standard units matter.
Reads the instrument carelessly — doesn't measure to the nearest mark, mis-reads the jug's meniscus or the scale.

learn.summary: Children aged 6–7 learn to measure in appropriate standard units: length (m/cm), mass (kg/g), temperature (°C) and capacity (litres/ml). The skill has two joined parts: first name the attribute (how long? how heavy? how much fills it? how hot?) so the unit family and instrument match, then choose the grain of unit that yields a readable, precise number (a pencil in cm, not m; a drink in ml, not litres), and read the instrument to the nearest sensible mark.

activities.title: Measuring station: choose the tool and the unit
feedback: If a learner dials the pencil to metres and reads '0 m', ask: does that number tell us anything useful? Prompt them to choose a smaller unit so the number becomes readable.
If a learner reaches for the ruler to measure the water, ask: does a ruler tell us how MUCH liquid there is, or just how tall the jug is? Redirect to the measuring jug and millilitres.

When a learner picks cm for the pencil and m for the table, confirm: you matched the unit to the size so the number is easy to read and sensible for that object (and if a more exact table length is needed, centimetres can be used too).
If a learner can measure but cannot say why cm rather than m, ask them to compare the two readings and name which is sensible for this object.
activities.rationale: Making the choice of instrument and unit the practised act — and letting a bad choice produce an awkward or impossible reading — is intended to rehearse grain judgement and attribute-matching directly, rather than only reading a pre-chosen tool. An optional interactive version can recompute the readout live as the unit dial turns so the awkward-to-clean transition is immediate; the same learning can be done with real instruments and objects.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils choose and use appropriate standard units to estimate and measure length/height (m/cm), mass (kg/g), temperature (°C) and capacity (litres/ml) to the nearest appropriate unit, using rulers, scales, thermometers and measuring vessels.

Measuring length consists of choosing a unit of measure and iterating it along the object; second graders select and use appropriate tools such as rulers, metre sticks and measuring tapes (2.MD.1). Children may not appreciate the need for identical, standard units and will even measure with a tool subdivided into different-sized units and conclude quantities with more units are larger; establishing why standard units are needed is central.
learnerActions: Set out a mixed set of objects one at a time — a pencil, a table, an apple, a jug of juice, a cup of water (and, if available, something whose temperature matters) — with a ruler/tape, a kitchen scale, a measuring jug and a thermometer all available.
For each object, first say out loud what KIND of measurement this is: how long? how heavy? how much fills it? how hot?
Pick the matching instrument, then choose the standard unit (m or cm, kg or g, litres or ml, °C).
Measure to the nearest mark and state the amount with its unit.

Try a deliberate mismatch — measure the pencil in metres — and notice the number is useless (to the nearest metre a pencil rounds to '0 m'); then switch to centimetres and get a clean reading (a real pencil is usually somewhere between about 10 cm and 19 cm, depending on how much it has been sharpened).
Try reaching for the ruler to measure the jug of juice and notice it cannot give a capacity reading at all.
activities.intendedInsight: You first decide what kind of quantity you are measuring so the unit family and tool fit, then choose a unit grain that gives a sensible, readable number.

activities.title: Why standard units at all — the hand-span contrast
feedback: If a learner is untroubled that the two hand-span counts differ, ask: if you and a friend measured the same table, should you get the same answer? Why didn't you?
If a learner reports a non-standard count ('6 cubes') when a standard unit was asked for, point back to the hand-span contrast and ask which answer another person could check.
activities.rationale: Contrasting two people's hand-spans on the same object is intended to surface the misconception that a personal or non-standard count is sufficient, and to motivate why standard units matter before they are relied on.
sourceClaims: Measuring length consists of choosing a unit of measure and iterating it along the object; second graders select and use appropriate tools such as rulers, metre sticks and measuring tapes (2.MD.1). Children may not appreciate the need for identical, standard units and will even measure with a tool subdivided into different-sized units and conclude quantities with more units are larger; establishing why standard units are needed is central.
learnerActions: Measure the same object (e.g. a table) in hand-spans with two different people and record both counts — for example one person gets 8, another gets 9.
Discuss why the two counts differ for the same table.
Re-measure with a ruler in centimetres and compare: everyone gets the same number.
Explain in your own words why we use standard units like centimetres instead of hand-spans or cubes.
activities.intendedInsight: Standard units let everyone agree and compare, because a non-standard unit changes from person to person.

activities.title: Sort objects to their sensible unit
feedback: If a learner picks kg for an apple, compare the apple against a 1 kg bag benchmark and ask whether the apple is about that heavy.
If a learner sorts a pencil under metres, ask them to picture a metre stick and judge whether the pencil is close to that length.
activities.rationale: Sorting objects to units and choosing the best unit checks the judgement that underlies the choosing skill and is strongly discriminating; it verifies the decision rather than rehearsing the physical act of measuring, so use it alongside hands-on measuring, not instead of it.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils choose and use appropriate standard units to estimate and measure length/height (m/cm), mass (kg/g), temperature (°C) and capacity (litres/ml) to the nearest appropriate unit, using rulers, scales, thermometers and measuring vessels.
learnerActions: Sort a set of everyday objects under the unit you would use: m, cm, kg, g, litres, ml, °C.
Answer targeted questions such as 'Which unit would you use to weigh an apple?' and justify the choice, rejecting a too-big option like kilograms in favour of grams.
Pair each unit with a benchmark object (a metre stick, a 1 kg bag, a 1 litre bottle) and use the benchmark to sanity-check your sorting.
activities.intendedInsight: Each attribute and each sensible size has a matching unit family and grain, which a benchmark size helps you judge.

activities.title: Benchmark reference card
feedback: If a learner is unsure of a unit, direct them to the benchmark and ask: is the object about this big/heavy, or much bigger/smaller?
activities.rationale: A reference chart supports unit choice as a reminder, but it cannot let a learner make and test a choice; it is a scaffold to use alongside active measuring, not a substitute for it.
learnerActions: Keep a reference chart beside your measuring that pairs each unit with a benchmark size and example objects (a metre stick for m, a 1 kg bag for kg, a 1 litre bottle for litres).
Reveal each pairing and use it to check whether your chosen unit looks right for the object in front of you.
activities.intendedInsight: Anchoring each unit to a familiar benchmark size helps you judge which unit gives a readable number.

activities.title: Read the instrument to the nearest mark
feedback: If a learner reads the jug from above or below eye level, show that the line appears to move; have them bring their eyes level with the liquid surface.
If a learner reads off the wrong mark, have them find the nearest marked line and read again. Do not reteach unit choice — that skill is intact here.
activities.rationale: Careless reading is a performance slip separate from unit choice; scaffolding accurate reading addresses it without undoing the choosing skill the learner already has.
learnerActions: With the correct tool and unit already chosen, read a ruler, scale, measuring jug and thermometer carefully.
Read the measuring jug at eye level and find the liquid line (meniscus).
Round to the nearest marked line rather than guessing a whole number.
State the measurement precisely with its unit.
activities.intendedInsight: Even with the right tool and unit, the reading must be taken to the nearest mark and from the correct line to be accurate.

constraints: Introduce standard units once the need for them is understood; heavy early use of many varied non-standard units, before the purpose of measurement is grasped, can interfere with understanding why standard units are needed.
Sorting and targeted-question checks verify the judgement of which unit to use but do not rehearse the physical act of measuring; pair them with hands-on measuring.
A reference card reminds learners of benchmarks but cannot let them make and test a choice; it is a scaffold, not the core activity.
Assessment is best done by watching the learner choose the tool and unit across a mixed set of objects, not by asking them to recite rules.
An interactive live-recompute station is one way to make a bad grain visibly awkward; real instruments and objects achieve the same learning and should not be treated as replaceable by a screen only.

Choosing units is primarily a categorical/attribute judgement; a spatial 3D setting may offer little specific additional leverage for it, and in-role dialogue can discuss but not itself rehearse the watched act of picking a tool — these are observations about fit, not claims that any medium is necessary or impossible.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source row claimed a 3D environment 'adds no insight' and that in-role dialogue 'cannot rehearse' the skill. These were catalogue fit judgements, not established facts, and have been reframed as narrow, qualified affordance observations rather than universal claims of necessity or impossibility.
The '0 m' and ~'13 cm' pencil examples and the 8-vs-9 hand-span counts are illustrative; real measurements vary, so treat specific numbers as examples to be replaced by actual readings.

The UK National Curriculum source claim is marked verified:false in the source row; its content is retained as cited (it is the only claim covering all four attributes) but is not independently confirmed in this rewrite and should not be read as verified.

The Grade 1 interference claim was not attached to the hand-span activity's sourceClaims because it supports the deferral constraint, not that activity's stated rationale; it remains embodied in the constraints.

probeDeeper: Why did you choose centimetres and not metres for the pencil?
If I asked you to measure the length of the playground, would you still use centimetres? What would you use instead, and why?
Which of these tools tells you how HEAVY the apple is, rather than how big it is?
Your friend measured the table in hand-spans and got 9, but you got 8. Who is right — and why do we bother using centimetres?
assess.correctAnswer: For each object the child identifies the attribute and selects a matching instrument, chooses a standard unit of an appropriate grain (cm for the pencil, m for the table/room, g for the apple, ml for the cup, litres for the jug), measures to the nearest unit, and states the amount with its unit — and can say why that unit rather than a much bigger or smaller one.

errorPatterns.pattern: Attribute–unit mismatch: uses a tool or unit from the wrong attribute — reaches for a ruler to find 'how much water', or reports grams for a length — not first asking what kind of quantity this is.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Name the attribute first (how long? how heavy? how much fills it? how hot?), then match the unit family; return to hands-on experience with the weak attribute (e.g. filling and pouring for capacity).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Picks up the ruler for the jug of juice, or answers a 'how heavy?' question in centimetres.

errorPatterns.pattern: Wrong grain — not the nearest appropriate unit: picks a unit far too big or small for the object, e.g. a pencil in metres or a room in centimetres, and doesn't notice the number is unusable.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Discuss which unit gives a sensible, readable number; anchor each unit to a benchmark size and sanity-check the result.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Reports '0 m' for a pencil, or sets out to measure the room in centimetres; accepts a nonsense-sized number.

errorPatterns.pattern: Doesn't see the need for standard units: offers a non-standard count ('6 cubes', 'a jug-full') when a standard measurement is asked for, or invents a personal unit.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast two children's hand-spans giving different numbers for the same object; establish that standard units let everyone agree and compare.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives a non-standard answer to 'how many centimetres/grams/millilitres?'; untroubled that another child's count would differ.

errorPatterns.pattern: Careless reading — not to the nearest unit: chooses the right tool and unit but misreads the scale or jug (ignores the meniscus, doesn't round to the nearest mark).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold reading to the nearest mark and reading the jug at eye level; the choosing skill itself is intact, so do not reteach unit choice.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Right instrument and unit, but the number is read off imprecisely or from the wrong line.

responseLevels.gap: Uses a wrong-attribute tool or unit, or reports non-standard counts, or picks a grain that gives a nonsense number without noticing.
responseLevels.full: For each object names the attribute, selects a sensible instrument and an appropriate-grain standard unit, measures to the nearest unit, and justifies the choice (a readable, precise number) and why standard units are used at all.
responseLevels.partial: Matches the right attribute and a standard unit but not to the nearest appropriate grain — measures the room in cm or the pencil in m — succeeding where the unit is obvious but not where scale or precision must be judged.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Lay out a range of objects — a pencil, a table, an apple, a jug of juice, a cup of water (and, if you have one, something whose temperature matters) — with a ruler and tape, a scale, a measuring jug and a thermometer available. Say: 'Measure each of these and tell me the amount.' Do not tell them which tool or unit. Watch which instrument and unit they reach for, whether the grain fits, and how they read it.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands unit choice matches the tool to the attribute and dials the grain to a readable, precise number; a child who does not grabs a wrong-attribute tool, reports an awkward '0 m'-type figure without noticing, or offers a non-standard count — each visible in the act, none of which a child with the full concept does. It is watched, never asked about.
